claim: Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus (Pompey the Great) was born on 29 September 106 BCE in Picenum.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 1.1 for Picenum origin; birth date needs verification (Plutarch does not give exact date)

claim: His father was Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 1.1

claim: Pompeius Strabo became consul in 89 BCE.
passage_ref: needs_verification: exact ancient passage for Strabo's consulship date

claim: Pompeius Strabo was the first of his branch of the Pompeia gens to achieve senatorial status in Rome.
passage_ref: needs_verification: Plutarch, Life of Pompey likely mentions Strabo's novus homo status

claim: Pompey began his military career serving with his father during the Social War (91-87 BCE).
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 3; Leach p.13

claim: After his father's death in 87 BCE, Pompey was put on trial as Strabo's legal heir for alleged embezzlement and was acquitted.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 4

claim: In 83 BCE, Pompey raised a private legion from his father's veterans in Picenum to support Sulla in the civil war.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 6

claim: Sulla greeted Pompey with the title imperator upon his arrival at Sulla's camp in 83 BCE.
passage_ref: needs_verification: Plutarch, Life of Pompey ~8 mentions the greeting but exact wording needs verification against Greek text
uncertainty_note: Exact passage in ancient sources not verified. Plutarch Life of Pompey mentions the greeting but precise wording needs verification.

claim: Sulla persuaded Pompey to divorce his first wife Antistia and marry his stepdaughter Aemilia Scaura.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 9

claim: Pompey campaigned successfully in Sicily (82-81 BCE) against Marian holdouts, executing Gnaeus Papirius Carbo.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 10

claim: In 81 BCE, Pompey defeated Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus at the Battle of Utica in Africa and subdued Numidia.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 12

claim: During the African campaign, his troops began calling him Magnus (the Great), in reference to Alexander the Great. Pompey later formally adopted this as his cognomen.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 13 for troops calling him Magnus
uncertainty_note: Ancient sources differ on whether Sulla or Pompey's troops first used the title Magnus.

claim: Sulla's opponents nicknamed Pompey adulescentulus carnifex (teenage butcher) due to his perceived ruthlessness.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 10; also attested in other sources
uncertainty_note: The nickname is attested in hostile sources; its accuracy as a description of Pompey's character is a matter of interpretation.

claim: Pompey demanded a triumph for his African victories despite being too young and not holding any elected office, an unprecedented demand that Sulla eventually granted.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 14

claim: Pompey married Mucia Tertia of the Metellus family and had three children: Gnaeus Pompeius (the younger), Pompeia Magna, and Sextus Pompey.
passage_ref: needs_verification: Plutarch mentions the marriage and children but exact passage references need verification

claim: Pompey suppressed Marcus Aemilius Lepidus's rebellion in 77 BCE, besieging and capturing Mutina where Marcus Junius Brutus (father of Caesar's assassin) surrendered and was killed.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 15-16

claim: Pompey commanded Roman forces in the Sertorian War in Hispania (76-71 BCE), ultimately defeating Quintus Sertorius's successors after Sertorius was assassinated by his own officer Perperna.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 17-21

claim: Returning from Hispania in 71 BCE, Pompey intercepted and killed 6,000 fugitives from Spartacus's defeated slave army.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 21.2

claim: Pompey claimed credit for ending the Third Servile War based on his interception of Spartacus's fugitives.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 21.2

claim: Pompey's claim of credit for ending the Third Servile War caused lasting resentment from Crassus, who had defeated Spartacus's main army.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Crassus, 11.7; Life of Pompey, 21.2
uncertainty_note: Plutarch records this resentment but the emotional impact is Plutarch's interpretation.

claim: Pompey and Marcus Licinius Crassus were elected consuls for 70 BCE, despite Pompey being technically ineligible due to age and never having held lower offices.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 22; Livy, Periochae, 97.6

claim: During their consulship in 70 BCE, Pompey and Crassus restored the powers of the plebeian tribunes that Sulla had removed.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 22; Livy, Periochae, 97.6

claim: In 67 BCE, the Lex Gabinia granted Pompey extraordinary command over the Mediterranean to eliminate piracy, which he achieved in approximately three months.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 25-26; Cassius Dio, 36.20-37

claim: In 66 BCE, the Lex Manilia gave Pompey command against Mithridates VI of Pontus, replacing Lucullus.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 30; Cicero, Pro Lege Manilia (speech in support)

claim: Pompey defeated Mithridates VI of Pontus, who later died in 63 BCE.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 32-33; Cassius Dio, 36.48-50

claim: Pompey reorganized the Roman East after the Third Mithridatic War, establishing provinces and client kingdoms.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 38-42; Cassius Dio, 37.7a-20

claim: Pompey annexed Syria as a Roman province in 64 BCE after the collapse of the Seleucid Empire.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 39; Josephus, Antiquities, 14.29-34

claim: In 63 BCE, Pompey intervened in the Hasmonean Civil War in Judaea, supporting Hyrcanus II against Aristobulus II.
passage_ref: Josephus, Antiquities, 14.29-46; Jewish War, 1.127-132

claim: Pompey besieged Jerusalem for three months before capturing it in 63 BCE.
passage_ref: Josephus, Antiquities, 14.54-66; Jewish War, 1.145-151

claim: Upon capturing the Jerusalem Temple, Pompey entered the Holy of Holies, an act regarded as a desecration.
passage_ref: Josephus, Antiquities, 14.71-73; Jewish War, 1.152-153

claim: Pompey installed Hyrcanus II as high priest and client ruler of Judaea but denied him the title of king, and reduced Judaea's territory.
passage_ref: Josephus, Antiquities, 14.73-79; Jewish War, 1.153-158

claim: In 60 BCE, Pompey, Julius Caesar, and Marcus Licinius Crassus formed the First Triumvirate, an informal political alliance to dominate Roman politics.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 46-47; Life of Caesar, 13-14

claim: The Triumvirate was sealed by Pompey's marriage to Caesar's daughter Julia in 59 BCE.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 47; Life of Caesar, 14

claim: Pompey celebrated his third triumph in 61 BCE for his eastern victories.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 45
uncertainty_note: Ancient sources describe the triumph as exceptionally magnificent, but such descriptions are conventional and may be exaggerated.

claim: Pompey and Crassus served as consuls again in 55 BCE after the Conference of Luca renewed the Triumvirate.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 51-52

claim: Julia, Pompey's wife and Caesar's daughter, died in childbirth in 54 BCE, weakening the bond between Pompey and Caesar.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 53; Life of Caesar, 23.5-6

claim: Crassus died at the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BCE fighting the Parthians, removing the third member of the Triumvirate.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Crassus, 25-33; Life of Pompey, 53

claim: In 52 BCE, Pompey was elected sole consul (consul sine collega) to restore order after widespread political violence, an unprecedented constitutional arrangement.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 54-55

claim: After Julia's death, Pompey married Cornelia Metella, daughter of Metellus Scipio and widow of Publius Crassus (son of Marcus Crassus).
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 55

claim: After the deaths of Julia (54 BCE) and Crassus (53 BCE), Pompey aligned himself with the optimates (conservative senatorial faction) against Caesar.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 56-57
uncertainty_note: Pompey's alignment with the optimates is the consensus of modern scholarship but the label optimates is a modern analytical category; Pompey's exact relationship with specific senatorial groups varied.

claim: The Senate declared Caesar a public enemy on 7 January 49 BCE, leading to Caesar crossing the Rubicon and starting the civil war.
passage_ref: Caesar, De Bello Civili, 1.1-8; Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 59-60

claim: Pompey withdrew from Italy to Greece in 49 BCE to regroup his forces, a strategic retreat that surprised Caesar.
passage_ref: Caesar, De Bello Civili, 1.24-30; Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 62-63

claim: Pompey was decisively defeated by Caesar at the Battle of Pharsalus on 9 August 48 BCE despite having a larger army.
passage_ref: Caesar, De Bello Civili, 3.82-99; Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 68-72

claim: After the Battle of Pharsalus, Pompey fled to Egypt seeking refuge.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 73-77; Caesar, De Bello Civili, 3.102-104

claim: Pompey was assassinated on 28 September 48 BCE at Pelusium by agents of Ptolemy XIII.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 77-80; Caesar, De Bello Civili, 3.104

claim: Pompey was killed by Lucius Septimius, a Roman officer serving in the Egyptian army who had previously served under Pompey.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 78-79

claim: Pompey's body was cremated by his servants on the beach; his head was kept as evidence for Caesar and later returned to his widow Cornelia for burial.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 80

claim: Pompey was an outstanding strategist and organizer who won campaigns through superior planning and maneuver rather than tactical brilliance in battle.
passage_ref: Modern scholarly assessment; not derived from any single ancient source passage
uncertainty_note: This assessment is a modern scholarly consensus, not an ancient source claim.

claim: Florus wrote: 'Pompey could not brook an equal, or Caesar a superior' (Pompeium non ferebat parem, nec Caesarem superiorem).
passage_ref: Florus, Epitome of Roman History, 2.13.14
uncertainty_note: Exact chapter/verse reference 2.13.14 needs verification against critical edition.

claim: Pompey built Rome's first permanent stone theatre, the Theatre of Pompey, dedicated in 55 BCE on the Campus Martius.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 52

claim: The Roman Senate met in the Curia of Pompey's theatre complex, where Julius Caesar was assassinated in 44 BCE at the foot of Pompey's statue.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Caesar, 66; Life of Brutus, 17

claim: Pompey's original nomen was simply Gnaeus Pompeius; Magnus (the Great) was added later as a cognomen.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 13 for adoption of Magnus

claim: Pompey reformed provincial administration in the East, establishing the provinces of Bithynia and Pontus, Syria, and reorganizing Cilicia.
passage_ref: Cassius Dio, 37.7a-20; Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 38-42

claim: Pompey's eastern settlement significantly increased Roman state revenues through tribute and taxes from newly organized provinces and client kingdoms.
passage_ref: Plutarch, Life of Pompey, 45; Pliny the Elder, Natural History, 7.97 for revenue figures
